newsitem.title: USA: CIGNA sees '98 earnings ahead of avg forecast.
newsitem.headline: CIGNA sees '98 earnings ahead of avg forecast.

text.p: CIGNA Corp said it expects its 1998 earnings to exceed Wall Street's average estimate as a result of the acquisition of Healthsource Inc.
The First Call consensus estimate for 1998 is $15.23 a share.
CIGNA declined to provide an estimate of 1998 earnings or much guidance for 1997 earnings.

However, CIGNA chief financial officer James Stewart, speaking on an conference call, said that relative to analysts's average estimate, "we expect the transaction will add to 1998 earnings per share."
CIGNA also told analysts they could assume the company would not buy back any additional stock in 1997 and 1998 as it uses the capital for the acquisition instead.
CIGNA, which earlier said it had a definitive agreement to buy Healthsource in a deal worth $1.7 billion, said it plans to pay for the acquisition with about $400 million cash on hand.

CIGNA also plans to borrow in the long-term markets about $650 million and pay for the balance with short-term bridge financing, which the company plans to pay off in 1998 with 1997 and 1998 cash flow, Stewart said.
He said the company expects $65 million in annual after-tax interest expense related to the debt financing.
In addition to the debt costs, Stewart said the transaction should create about $1.3 billion of good will.
He said the company expects to write off the good will over 25 years, resulting in after-tax charges of about $50 million a year.
CIGNA chief executive Wilson Taylor described the acquisition as a great fit, giving CIGNA access to a number of new states and an opportunity to improve revenue and profit margins.

"We do believe big is better in this business," Taylor said on the conference call. "And in the case of Healthsource, we get more lives and attractive locations and the business will clearly add to our existing customer base," he said.
Taylor said the company will acquire a new presence in six states, four with a major HMO presence. The deal also will give CIGNA a much stronger presence in the southeastern United States.
CIGNA will gain immediate access to some new states, which are relatively underpenetrated, such as Maine, New Hampshire, South Carolina and Arkansas, he said.
He said CIGNA also will acquire meaningful membership gains in Tennessee, North Carolina and Massachusetts.
Taylor said the company expects to achieve $75 million pre-tax in cost savings from the consolidation of operations.
CIGNA said the closing was subject to regulatory approvals. The company declined to project a closing date, but said the approvals were likely to take at least 60 days.
After completion of the deal, CIGNA's debt-to-capital ratio will rise to about 25 percent compared to a current level in the high teens, Stewart said.
However, the debt-to-capital ratio will gradually decline to around 20 percent as the company pays off the short-term bridge financing, he said.

Stewart declined to say whether the acquisition would result in a dilution of the company's 1997 earnings. He advised analysts to maintain their current estimates until the company could provide them with further information.
The First Call consensus for 1997 is $14.03 a share, compared to 1996 earnings of $13.14 a share.
For 1998, in the HMO business, Stewart said CIGNA expects Healthsource's margins to move closer to CIGNA's margins of about five percent pre-tax.
CIGNA said it expects annual HMO revenue growth of 10 to 15 percent through 1998 and said Healthsource had 1996 HMO revenues of about $1.2 billion.
CIGNA said it assumes it will retain about 90 percent of Healthsource's HMO book of business.
On the indemnity business, CIGNA said it expects 1998 pre-tax margins of 2.5-3.0 percent, and expects premiums and premium equivalents to decline by about five percent a year.

Pricing appeared to improve in the 1996 January renewal season, Stewart said. Current indications are that pricing in the January renewal cycle went up three to four percent, compared with a decline in pricing in January 1996, he said.
In addition, he said, important re-underwriting steps were taken relative to some underperforming operations.
((--Patricia Vowinkel 212-859-1716))
